For conversational feed controls, generate a structured preference object rather than allowing arbitrary model output to become executable ranking code. Validate supported fields and show the interpreted intent to the viewer.

Creation provenance

A generated clip, voice, or edited segment needs lineage: source assets, consent, tool and model versions, transformations, and disclosure state. Preserve provenance through export and re-upload where technically possible, while acknowledging that metadata can be stripped and cannot alone prove authenticity.

A creator can approve a generated draft without granting unrestricted future use of their likeness or voice. Store consent scopes and revocation behavior. Sensitive likeness or realistic synthetic content requires additional policy and review, not just an attractive generation interface.

On-device versus server execution

On-device effects reduce round-trip latency and can improve privacy, but face memory, thermal, and battery constraints. Server models offer more capacity but introduce network delay, cost, and data-handling obligations. A hybrid can use lightweight local previews and heavier optional processing, with consistent provenance and fallback behavior.

Evaluation

Measure factual grounding, unsafe tool attempts, unauthorized data exposure, latency, cost, and user correction rates. Test prompt injection in captions and comments, missing sources, conflicting rights, and stale Studio permissions. An assistant's success rate must include its refusal to perform unauthorized actions, not only the number of completed tool calls.

Back to contents

Data platforms and machine learning

CHAPTER 49

Metadata storage, sharding, and the Vitess history

Choose consistency by invariant, then choose a storage engine.

Historical evidence

Vitess originated at YouTube to address MySQL scaling and sharding. Its current project documentation explains a routing and management layer for sharded MySQL. This history does not establish that every present-day YouTube metadata service uses Vitess or the same schema. [52] [53]

A proposed storage portfolio

Use transactional storage for channel membership, publication pointers, policy state, and financial obligations. Use object storage for large immutable media. Use specialized indexes for search and vector retrieval. Use append-oriented event storage for analytics and audit. A single database can serve several early needs, but one consistency model should not be forced onto every workload.

Start with explicit access patterns. A video page reads one video and related metadata; a channel list scans by channel and publication time; a rights operation may affect many videos; a history query scans by account. These access patterns suggest different indexes and partition keys.

Shard selection

A channel-based shard localizes creator operations but can create hot shards for enormous channels. A video-hash shard distributes traffic but makes channel scans cross-shard. A hybrid can separate authoritative per-video state from a channel-list projection. Make the tradeoff explicit rather than claiming consistent hashing solves every access pattern.

Keep hot mutable counters out of the main video row. A popular video's view count should not serialize all metadata reads and writes. Aggregate counters in a separate pipeline, then publish bounded-freshness display values.

Cross-shard transactions

Avoid distributing a transaction merely because services have different names. Keep tightly coupled invariants within one ownership boundary when possible. When a cross-shard transaction is necessary, use a storage system that supports it or a carefully specified workflow with compensation. Compensation is not equivalent to atomicity for irreversible external effects.

Spanner's published design illustrates globally coordinated transactions and external consistency, but adopting a distributed database does not eliminate latency, quorum, or partition tradeoffs. [62]

Resharding

A safe migration copies a snapshot, streams changes, validates checksums and logical counts, shadows reads, then moves authority under a controlled version. Prevent simultaneous writers from diverging during cutover. Keep rollback semantics clear: after new writes land on the destination, rolling back routing may require reverse replication rather than simply flipping a flag.

Validation gate

Load-test a viral video, a large creator's bulk edit, a rights action spanning shards, and a shard migration. Verify that a hot projection does not block publication authority and that every acknowledged mutation survives the supported failure model.

Back to contents

Data platforms and machine learning

CHAPTER 50

Media objects, Colossus, and storage lifecycle

Large immutable media needs integrity, placement, and deletion policies beyond a file path.

Published infrastructure

Google's Colossus material describes a distributed storage foundation and explicitly names YouTube video storage as a workload. The sources discuss placement and storage tiers; they do not justify describing YouTube as an ordinary retail Cloud Storage customer. [58] [59]

Proposed object model

An object record contains digest, length, media role, storage class, encryption context, creation lineage, and retention state. A logical release references objects by identity. Storage locations are replaceable implementation details; moving an object between tiers should not change its content identity.

Verify integrity at upload, transformation, replication, and periodic scrubbing. A successful write acknowledgment is not permanent proof against later corruption. Keep enough redundancy and independent validation to repair damaged replicas before multiple failures accumulate.

Replication and coding

Replication offers simple reads and repair at a high capacity cost. Erasure coding can reduce storage overhead but changes repair bandwidth, read amplification, and failure behavior. Select policies by access frequency, object size, latency needs, and recovery requirements. Do not apply the same storage policy to a tiny manifest and a large cold source asset merely for uniformity.

Store high-demand derived media near serving paths while retaining original sources according to the product and legal policy. Re-encoding can recover a missing derived object only if the source, recipe, and required tools remain available. Treat those dependencies as part of durability planning.

Lifecycle economics

A long-tail catalog accumulates storage even when new uploads are modest. Track source bytes, derivative multiplier, replication/coding overhead, abandoned attempts, and retained old releases. Garbage collection of orphaned work can be a major cost lever, but it must never race active publication or offline references.

A popularity-based tiering policy should include retrieval latency and rehydration cost. Moving an object to cold storage immediately before a sudden viral spike can create an origin bottleneck. Keep a rapid promotion path and observe miss amplification.

Deletion and holds

Separate ordinary garbage collection from privacy deletion, creator deletion, rights evidence retention, and legal holds. A hold must be narrowly scoped and audited. A deletion plan should enumerate replicas, caches, indexes, derived assets, and backup policy, while acknowledging bounded residual copies where applicable.

Failure exercise

Corrupt one replica, remove a storage zone, lose a derived representation, and run garbage collection during a release update. Verify repair, checksum detection, reconstruction, and reference safety. Count a restore as successful only when playable content, publication pointers, and current denies agree.

Back to contents

Data platforms and machine learning

CHAPTER 51

Zanzibar and causally consistent authorization

Permission decisions must not move backward relative to content changes.

Published design

Zanzibar's paper describes relationship-based authorization and consistency tokens that help coordinate content and permission changes. YouTube is a named client. Its reported component performance belongs to that paper and is not a YouTube-wide service guarantee. [54] [55]

The stale-permission problem

Imagine a private video shared with an editor. The owner removes the editor and then updates sensitive metadata. If a content service reads the new metadata but checks permission against an older authorization snapshot, the removed editor may see the new content. This is an ordering failure, not merely a slow cache.

A reference design associates a content revision with a minimum authorization-consistency token. A read must evaluate access at a snapshot no older than that bound. The content store records the token together with the revision so the relationship survives retries and replication.

What the token does not solve

The bound prevents authorization from being older than a required causal point. It does not automatically include every later revocation. For new playback grants, enforce an additional current-policy freshness requirement or deny-epoch check. For ongoing grants, state the expiry and refresh behavior. Do not claim instantaneous revocation from the existence of a consistency token alone.

Relationship model

Relations can express channel owner, editor, viewer, group membership, and content sharing. Permission expressions combine those relations. Keep the model understandable and bounded: deeply recursive relationships or unconstrained group expansion can create unpredictable latency.

Cache decisions with the relevant relation and policy versions, and avoid reusing an allow result across different content revisions or viewer contexts. A cache key missing the acting channel can become a cross-tenant data leak even when the policy engine itself is correct.

Write protocol

An authorized metadata mutation checks actor permission, applies the content change under an expected version, and records the required authorization token. Sensitive permission changes should produce an audit event and invalidate affected decision caches. The exact distributed transaction arrangement depends on the chosen storage and authorization services; document the failure window rather than hiding it behind an API call.

Failure behavior

If the authorization service cannot satisfy the required freshness, retry or deny according to the operation's safety requirements. A public thumbnail read may tolerate different staleness from a private Studio revenue report. Scope the policy to the resource and action.

Validation gate

Reorder permission removal, metadata publication, replica reads, and cache refreshes. Test groups, delegated channels, and stale sessions. The system must prevent a newer protected content revision from being served using older permission evidence, while separately honoring the defined bound for subsequent revocations.

Back to contents

Data platforms and machine learning

CHAPTER 52

Event logs, outboxes, deduplication, and replay

Exactly-once business effects require more than choosing a message broker.

Design status

This chapter proposes a generic durable event architecture. It does not claim that YouTube universally uses a particular public broker or that one messaging product supplies end-to-end exactly-once behavior.

Transactional outbox

When publication changes, commit the new state and an outbox record in one database transaction. A relay publishes that record to the event system. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking it sent, the event may be delivered again. Consumers therefore need stable event identities and idempotent processing.

Do not write the database and then independently send a message without a recovery mechanism. A crash between those operations can leave search, notifications, and analytics permanently unaware of a committed change.

Consumer transaction

For a transactional projection, insert a receipt keyed by (consumer, event_id), apply the projection update, and advance durable progress atomically where the storage model permits. A duplicate receipt becomes a no-op. When an event carries a resource version, reject older versions so replay cannot undo a newer state.

External side effects such as push notifications need their own idempotency or delivery record. A broker's processing guarantee does not make a third-party API call exactly once. Separate "event consumed" from "external effect confirmed."

Ordering

Partition by the key whose order matters, such as video or broadcast. Global ordering is usually unnecessary and expensive. Cross-entity workflows need explicit dependencies or versions rather than assuming all events arrive in the order they were created.

An event envelope should include schema version, event ID, aggregate ID and version, event time, producer, trace context, and privacy classification. Avoid embedding large media or unnecessary personal data in a widely replicated log.

Replay and deletion

Replays are normal operations for index rebuilding and new projections. They must respect current tombstones and privacy constraints. A new consumer reading years of events should not resurrect deleted viewing history or removed videos. Maintain deletion generations and filter or transform historical data according to the retention policy.

Schema evolution needs compatibility tests. Adding an optional field is different from changing the meaning of a metric or identifier. Store semantic versions and migration rules, not just a serialization schema.

Backpressure

Bound producer and consumer queues. Track oldest unprocessed event, lag by partition, retry rate, and dead-letter volume. A poison event must be isolated with an auditable exception path; endlessly retrying it can block unrelated work.

Production gate

Crash after every database and broker boundary, duplicate and reorder messages, introduce a new schema, replay after deletion, and stall one partition. The authoritative state remains correct, and derived systems converge without duplicate business effects.

Back to contents

Data platforms and machine learning

CHAPTER 53

Procella and serving analytical data

Creator dashboards need fresh, interactive analytics without querying raw events on every click.

Published architecture

The 2019 Procella paper describes a YouTube analytical engine supporting both serving and analytical workloads. Its architecture includes columnar Artus files on Colossus, metadata services, query roots and data servers, and a path for fresh ingestion. This is a dated published design, not a full inventory of current YouTube analytics. [56] [57]

A reference analytics stack

Raw validated events enter durable storage. Stream jobs compute near-real-time aggregates; batch jobs reconcile and build compact columnar datasets. A query layer serves creator dashboards and internal analysis with authorization, semantic definitions, and query budgets. Keep raw receipts, qualified events, aggregates, and financial results as distinguishable layers.

Columnar layouts help queries that scan a few fields across many rows. Partition by useful time and ownership dimensions, but avoid creating millions of tiny partitions. Use clustering, statistics, and aggregate materializations for common dashboard shapes.

Freshness versus consistency

A dashboard may combine a fresh streaming estimate with a settled historical segment. Mark the boundary and avoid double counting data present in both. Use ingestion watermarks or explicit overlap reconciliation. A query that reads some partitions before compaction and others after it needs a consistent manifest or snapshot contract.

Expose freshness and provisional status. A creator should know whether today's count is a near-real-time estimate or a finalized report. Hiding this distinction creates support incidents whenever late events or fraud corrections change the number.

Multi-tenant safety

A creator query must be constrained to authorized channels and permitted dimensions. Enforce this in the query service, not only in the dashboard UI. Apply per-tenant resource limits, result-size caps, and cancellation so one expensive report cannot starve everyone else.

Sensitive slices may require aggregation thresholds or suppressed results. Query logs themselves can contain private identifiers or search text; minimize and protect them.

Semantic layer

Define each metric's numerator, denominator, event version, allowed dimensions, currency, timezone, and correction rules. A report that mixes event time with receipt time can create misleading daily spikes. A report that sums distinct viewers across countries can double count people who appear in several groups.

Recovery and validation

Rebuild a sampled creator report from immutable source events and compare it with serving results. Test late arrivals, duplicate events, partition replacement, schema changes, and access revocation. A fast SQL response is not sufficient if it combines incompatible metric definitions or leaks another channel's data.

Back to contents

Data platforms and machine learning

CHAPTER 54

Feature pipelines and point-in-time training data

Offline model quality is meaningless when training sees information serving could not have known.

Research context

Published neural retrieval and multitask ranking work motivates large-scale feature and label pipelines. The platform architecture below is an original implementation proposal, not a claim about a named private YouTube feature store. [38] [37]

Feature contracts

A feature has an owner, entity key, type, units, computation version, event-time semantics, freshness target, default behavior, and privacy classification. Examples include recent video interactions, language preferences, content embeddings, and channel-level aggregates. Store missingness explicitly; zero is not always a safe substitute for unknown.

Use the same transformation logic or rigorously tested equivalent logic in training and serving. A subtle difference in tokenization, normalization, or time windows can create training-serving skew even when both pipelines are individually correct.

Point-in-time joins

For an impression at time t, join only feature values available by t under the defined observation delay. Do not attach a video's eventual popularity to an earlier recommendation. For late events, retain both event time and availability time so the training pipeline can model what the online system actually knew.

Labels also mature over time. A short watch may be known quickly; a later survey or return behavior arrives later. Define label windows and censoring. Treat examples without mature labels carefully rather than labeling them as negative simply because the pipeline ran too soon.

Online state

Serve low-latency features from a bounded-freshness store with versioned schemas. A request should know which features are stale, absent, or defaulted. The model must have a tested fallback for those conditions. Feature-store availability should not force the system to return an empty homepage if a safe simpler recommendation path exists.

Backfills

A backfill is a new computation over historical data. It should write to a new version or partition set, validate results, and then promote a pointer. In-place mutation can make experiments irreproducible and cause serving to observe a mixture of old and new definitions.

Privacy lineage

Track which consent and deletion generations contributed to datasets. Restrict raw history access and use aggregated or pseudonymous features where possible. Retention rules apply to feature snapshots and training exports, not only to the original event log.

Validation gate

Create synthetic events with delayed arrival, future popularity, missing features, and a consent change. Verify that training examples use only permissible point-in-time information and that online defaults match the model's tested behavior. Record dataset and feature hashes so a result can be reproduced.

Back to contents

Data platforms and machine learning

CHAPTER 55

Model serving, compatibility, and rollout

Deploy the model together with the feature and index contracts it requires.

Evidence boundary

The recommendation papers establish historical model families. They do not disclose the complete present-day serving runtime. The release protocol here is proposed for a high-scale recommendation service. [36] [37]

A model release is a bundle

Package weights, feature schema, preprocessing, calibration, vocabulary, item-index compatibility, inference code, and fallback configuration. Sign and version the bundle. A model that expects a new feature name but receives an old default can return plausible-looking yet harmful results without crashing.

Use explicit compatibility checks before traffic. Retrieval query towers and item embeddings need matching spaces. Rankers need compatible feature distributions. A release should identify which index and feature versions it can consume.

Latency management

Set a request deadline and divide it across candidate generation, feature fetch, ranking, reranking, and response assembly. Use bounded batching where it improves accelerator efficiency without violating latency. Batch size is a queueing tradeoff, not a free throughput improvement.

Cache safe intermediate results by model and context version. Avoid caching personalized outputs under incomplete keys. A cache missing an age mode, language, or privacy context can serve inappropriate results even if the model is correct.

Degradation

Define fallback levels: full model, reduced feature set, simpler ranker, cached eligible slate, and nonpersonalized safe discovery. Each level should have measured quality and resource behavior. Do not discover during an incident that the fallback calls the same unavailable feature service.

Rollout sequence

Validate offline, replay historical requests, shadow live traffic without affecting users, canary a small cohort, run a controlled experiment, and expand gradually. Shadow inference still consumes resources and handles private data; budget and authorize it properly.

Monitor output distributions, feature missingness, latency, exposure concentration, and negative feedback. A healthy process and low error rate do not prove the recommendations are healthy. Automated rollback can use guardrails, but ambiguous product changes need human review.

Incident diagnosis

Record a compact decision trace: model version, candidate sources, major feature versions, policy filters, and fallback level. Avoid logging every sensitive raw feature. The goal is to reproduce a problematic decision under controlled access, not build an unrestricted archive of user behavior.

Production gate

Deploy a deliberately incompatible index, remove a feature, slow an accelerator pool, and corrupt a model artifact. The service should reject invalid bundles, degrade within its deadline, and never bypass eligibility filters to keep a latency chart green.

Back to contents

Data platforms and machine learning

CHAPTER 56

Model governance, multimodal understanding, and feedback loops

Better representations do not remove the need for lineage, evaluation, and user controls.

Research boundary

VideoPrism is published Google Research on visual representation learning. Its existence is not evidence that every YouTube recommendation, safety, or search surface uses it. Similarly, research on jointly considering creation and consumption does not establish a universal production objective. [28] [42]

Shared representations, distinct decisions

A video embedding may support retrieval, duplicate detection, topic analysis, or moderation triage. Those applications require different thresholds, labels, and accountability. Reusing an embedding does not justify reusing a decision policy. A similarity signal useful for discovery may be unsuitable as evidence of rights ownership.

Maintain a model registry with training data lineage, evaluation scope, intended uses, prohibited uses, owners, and rollback artifacts. Record which downstream services consume each representation. A model change can affect many products even when its API shape remains unchanged.

Feedback loops

Recommendations influence what gets watched; viewing influences training; creators adapt to exposure incentives. This loop can amplify popularity, narrow discovery, or reward misleading packaging. Evaluate distributional effects and long-term behavior, not only immediate accuracy on logs produced by the previous system.

Provide explicit user controls and respect them across retraining. A repeated "not interested" signal should not be erased by a weak similarity inference. Keep account-level preference deletion and history controls connected to the feature pipeline.

Evaluation coverage

Use test sets across languages, formats, duration, content quality, and creator maturity. Track known blind spots such as speech recognition errors, low-light footage, rapid cuts, and ambiguous context. Human evaluation should be structured and reviewed for consistency, not treated as infallible ground truth.

For generative summaries, evaluate support for each claim and correct attribution to the source. For dubbing, evaluate meaning, timing, and consent. For safety, evaluate false positives and false negatives with appeal outcomes. One generic "AI quality" score cannot replace these product-specific measures.

Governance workflow

Require approval for new sensitive data sources and materially new uses. Keep deployment records and rollback plans. A model that improves one metric but violates data-use constraints is not eligible for release. Audit access to training exports and derived embeddings because they can still reveal information about source material.

Production gate

Trace a changed representation through search, recommendations, moderation, and analytics. Verify that each consumer has compatible evaluation and a fallback. Then simulate a data deletion or revoked source license and confirm the lineage system identifies affected datasets and future processing obligations.

Back to contents

Infrastructure, reliability, and operating design

CHAPTER 57

Compute scheduling and the Borg lesson

Interactive playback control, live media, and background encoding need different resource contracts.

Published infrastructure

Borg's published papers describe large-scale cluster management at Google, including admission, scheduling, isolation, and evolving workload characteristics. They are general Google infrastructure evidence, not a current inventory of every YouTube deployment or scheduler setting. [60] [61]

Workload classes

Separate latency-sensitive control services, real-time live processing, batch encoding, analytical jobs, and model training. They have different deadlines and interruption tolerance. A live encoder cannot safely share the same preemption policy as a library re-encode that can restart tomorrow.

Reserve capacity for critical paths and admit batch work against remaining resources. Estimate CPU, memory, accelerator, disk, and network needs. Packing by CPU alone can create memory or network hotspots. Track actual use and adjust requests carefully; optimistic overcommit can improve utilization until a correlated event makes every workload peak together.

Placement and failure domains

Spread replicas across independent failure domains and avoid placing all redundant live pipelines on one shared dependency. Affinity can improve locality, but excessive affinity increases correlated failure risk. Include storage and network paths in placement reasoning, not only machine labels.

A cell is a bounded serving and operational domain with its own capacity and blast radius. Use cells when scale justifies them; a small startup can begin with one regional deployment across zones. The interface should permit later partitioning without prematurely building a global scheduler.

Autoscaling

Scale from work and latency signals, not CPU alone. Encoding needs queue work-seconds and deadline risk. Session services need request rate, concurrency, and tail latency. Chat gateways need connections and egress. Forecast scheduled events because reactive scaling may arrive after the first large wave.

Readiness means the process can perform its role, not merely accept a TCP connection. An encoder without a loaded codec or a ranker without its model should not receive traffic. Distinguish startup, readiness, and liveness checks to avoid restart loops during slow initialization.

Cost controls

Use lower-cost interruptible capacity only for jobs with checkpoint and retry semantics. Include failed attempts and checkpoint overhead in cost calculations. A cheap machine that repeatedly loses nearly completed long jobs may be more expensive than stable capacity.

Production gate

Preempt batch workers, drain a zone, exhaust an accelerator class, and trigger a premiere surge. Verify critical services retain capacity and background queues age predictably. Resource efficiency is valuable only while the product's deadlines and safety invariants remain intact.

Back to contents

Infrastructure, reliability, and operating design

CHAPTER 58

Dependency control, overload, and graceful degradation

Protect useful work instead of allowing retries to consume the whole platform.

SRE foundation

Google's overload guidance emphasizes admission control, load shedding, and controlled degradation. The policies here apply those principles to a proposed video platform; they are not claimed to be YouTube's private configuration. [65]

Classify requests

Playback authorization, active live publication, and emergency restrictions deserve different priority from thumbnail regeneration, historical reports, or recommendation experiments. Define priority classes and resource reservations. Priority without admission limits can still overload the system if every caller labels its work critical.

Use deadlines across service calls. A downstream request should inherit the remaining budget, not start a fresh full timeout at every hop. Cancel work that can no longer help the user. Bound concurrent requests and queues so overload becomes a controlled rejection rather than an eventual memory crash.

Degradation ladder

Serve a minimal watch page if comments or rich metadata are unavailable. Use a simpler recommendation slate if advanced ranking fails. Delay nonessential encodes and analytics backfills. Preserve current policy checks and accounting integrity; these are not optional decorations to skip for speed.

For media delivery, prefer a lower compatible representation or alternate cache when allowed. Do not repeatedly select an unavailable high-quality variant just because it has the highest nominal quality score.

Circuit breakers and retries

A circuit breaker should reduce pressure on a failing dependency, but its state and recovery policy must be designed. A global breaker can turn a local failure into a global outage. Use scoped breakers and probe recovery gradually.

Retries consume a budget shared across layers. Apply jitter and backoff to transient errors, and do not retry permanent validation or policy denials. A delayed status lookup is often safer than repeating a mutation after an uncertain response.

Fairness and abuse

Apply per-account, per-channel, per-project, and expensive-operation limits. Keep a separate allowance for status and recovery calls so users can discover the outcome of accepted work. A high-volume creator should not crowd out ordinary uploads, and a malicious client should not force expensive encoding merely by retrying.

Failure exercise

Introduce a slow metadata dependency, then observe whether connection pools, queues, and retries saturate unrelated services. The desired result is bounded degradation with useful work preserved. A system that remains technically "up" while every request waits beyond its deadline is not available in a meaningful sense.

Back to contents

Infrastructure, reliability, and operating design

CHAPTER 59

Multi-region recovery and authority restoration

Recover current authority, not just old data and working servers.

Infrastructure context

Spanner's published design explains coordinated replication and external consistency, while SRE guidance distinguishes service objectives from implementation choices. The regional strategy below is a proposed architecture with explicit tradeoffs, not a published YouTube disaster-recovery contract. [62] [64]

Different data classes

Immutable media can be replicated and served from multiple regions with relatively simple identity checks. Mutable publication, permission, rights, and financial state require coordinated authority. Recommendation features and analytics may tolerate bounded staleness. Treating all data as "eventually consistent" hides the most important failure risks.

Choose a write authority for each aggregate or shard. A failover must transfer that authority through a mechanism that prevents the old writer from committing afterward. Fencing tokens checked at the authoritative store are more reliable than assuming the old region is physically dead.

Recovery sequence

First establish which authority and log position are current. Restore storage and verify integrity. Replay current tombstones, deny decisions, permission changes, and financial adjustments. Rebuild derived indexes and caches. Only then reopen sensitive writes and new playback grants under the declared freshness rules.

A database restored from yesterday can be internally consistent and still unsafe because it predates takedowns or account revocations. Recovery must account for those newer decisions from independent durable records.

RPO and RTO

Recovery point objective concerns how much acknowledged data may be lost. Recovery time objective concerns when a capability returns. Neither is automatically zero because a system has replicas. Measure them under the actual failure scenario, including detection, authority transfer, cache warming, dependent services, and operator decisions.

For live media, distinguish received durable segments from content that never reached the platform. No backup can recreate an unreceived camera feed. For uploads, distinguish acknowledged chunks from bytes still buffered on a failed connection.

Read-only or degraded operation

During authority uncertainty, continue serving already authorized immutable media only within the permitted grant and policy freshness bounds. Pause publication or sensitive edits rather than accepting conflicting writes. A stale analytics dashboard may be acceptable if labeled; a stale permission grant may not be.

Production gate

Lose a region during publication, during a rights withdrawal, and after a live segment commit whose response was lost. Keep the old region running behind a partition. Demonstrate that no stale writer can overwrite current state and that restoration does not resurrect withdrawn access.

Back to contents

Infrastructure, reliability, and operating design

CHAPTER 60

Observability and quality of experience

A green server dashboard does not prove that viewers can watch.

Published foundation

Monarch is a published Google time-series monitoring system with regional collection and query architecture. Its existence illustrates large-scale observability infrastructure, but does not specify YouTube's complete dashboard set or product objectives. [63]

Three observation layers

Infrastructure telemetry measures resource use, errors, queue age, and network health. Service telemetry measures request outcomes, dependency latency, and state transitions. Client quality-of-experience telemetry measures first frame, stalls, seeks, decode errors, selected quality, and user-visible failures.

Correlate the layers with sampled session and trace identifiers, while limiting sensitive payloads. A segment's origin miss can explain a player stall; a policy deny can explain a failed start without being an infrastructure outage. The diagnostic system should preserve those distinctions.

Useful dimensions

Break down by app version, device model family, operating system, codec, region, ISP cohort, content type, and delivery path. Control cardinality: individual video IDs or sessions in every metric label can overwhelm a time-series system. Use logs and traces for high-cardinality investigation and metrics for stable aggregates.

Telemetry reliability

Clients may disconnect before sending failure reports. Use bounded local buffering, receipt deduplication, and sampling designed to preserve rare failures. Compare server-side start attempts with client acknowledgments to estimate missing observations. Do not assume absent telemetry means successful playback.

Protect the telemetry pipeline from event storms. A retry bug that emits thousands of errors per second per device can itself become an outage. Rate-limit locally, aggregate repeated signatures, and preserve a sample of detailed evidence.

Alerting

Alert on user-impacting symptoms and fast error-budget burn, then use cause metrics for diagnosis. Separate paging alerts from capacity trends and data-quality reports. A threshold that pages continuously during normal evening peaks will train operators to ignore it.

Include correctness monitors: publication references to missing objects, stale deny freshness, duplicate financial effects, live sequence conflicts, and deletion resurrection. These may not cause an immediate HTTP error but can be more serious than a latency spike.

Incident evidence

Keep a compact incident timeline with deployment changes, traffic shifts, authority transfers, and mitigation actions. Preserve relevant logs under controlled retention. Review whether the system made uncertainty visible or hid it behind retries and provisional dashboards.

Production gate

Break one device cohort, one ISP path, one codec recipe, and one telemetry consumer. Confirm the platform detects the affected users without requiring every global metric to fail, and that monitoring remains useful during the incident it is meant to diagnose.

Back to contents

Infrastructure, reliability, and operating design

CHAPTER 61

Delivery engineering, testing, and schema evolution

A safe release changes code, data, models, and device contracts together.

Design status

This chapter proposes a software-delivery system for a large media platform. It does not attribute a specific private repository layout, build tool, or deployment service to YouTube.

Reproducible builds

Pin toolchains, dependencies, codec libraries, model artifacts, and build inputs. Produce signed artifacts with provenance and a software bill of materials. Native media libraries deserve particular attention because they parse untrusted input and evolve independently of application code.

Build once and promote the same artifact through environments. Rebuilding for production can introduce untested differences. Keep configuration versioned separately, with validation and rollback.

Test layers

Unit tests verify algorithms and state transitions. Integration tests exercise storage, queues, and authorization. Media conformance tests decode real output. Device tests exercise actual clients. Load tests expose queueing and resource limits. Chaos tests validate recovery assumptions. No single layer substitutes for the others.

Use a representative media corpus covering variable frame rate, rotation, HDR, captions, multiple audio tracks, unusual durations, and damaged inputs. Include known expected failures. A pipeline that only handles ideal sample files is not ready for public uploads.

Schema changes

Use expand-and-contract migrations. Add compatible fields, deploy readers that tolerate both versions, backfill safely, switch writers, verify, then remove old fields only after old clients and consumers are gone. A television client may remain deployed much longer than a backend service.

Version event semantics as well as serialization. Changing a view definition without a new semantic version can silently corrupt analytics even if every message still parses.

Canary and rollback

Canary by meaningful cohorts: device, region, codec, channel type, and traffic pattern. Keep previous media recipes and model bundles available. Rollback may require a data repair or pointer change, not merely a code revert, if the release already wrote incompatible state.

For high-risk configuration, require review, staged rollout, and automated bounds. A single global flag that simultaneously changes grant lifetime, cache routing, and feature eligibility creates a large blast radius.

Developer experience

Provide local simulators for uploads, delayed jobs, duplicate events, and policy changes. Make the safe path easy: standard idempotency middleware, outbox helpers, typed error contracts, and test fixtures. Good platform tooling reduces the number of teams inventing subtly incompatible recovery behavior.

Production gate

Deploy an old client against a new server, replay old events into a new consumer, roll back after partial backfill, and rotate a media toolchain. The release process must preserve both compatibility and the ability to explain what changed.

Back to contents

Infrastructure, reliability, and operating design

CHAPTER 62

Security, secrets, and content supply-chain trust

Protect creators, viewers, infrastructure, and unreleased media through separate trust boundaries.

Interface and standards context

YouTube developer policies constrain public integrations, and EME specifies an interface for protected-media systems rather than a universal protection mechanism. The security architecture here is defensive reference design, not a description of private keys or bypass techniques. [69] [67]

Trust zones

Separate public ingress, media quarantine, processing workers, control services, financial systems, reviewer tools, and production administration. Give each workload the minimum credentials and network access required. An encoder should read one assigned source and write its attempt outputs, not browse all private videos or modify channel permissions.

Use short-lived workload credentials and audited secret access. Rotate signing keys with overlap sufficient for valid old grants, while maintaining an emergency revocation procedure. Public verification keys can be cached; private signing keys should be protected by a dedicated key service or hardware-backed boundary appropriate to the risk.

Creator account protection

High-value channels are attractive takeover targets. Protect recovery and delegation, detect unusual sensitive changes, and require stronger confirmation for ownership, payout, and destructive operations. Notify trusted contacts without revealing private details to a newly added untrusted actor.

Administrative support should use constrained tools with explicit reasons and audit. Avoid a universal "impersonate any user" capability. Emergency access needs short duration, approval, and post-use review.

Media and build supply chain

Validate uploaded files in sandboxes and patch parser dependencies. Sign build artifacts and model bundles. Restrict who can change encoding recipes, policy configuration, or package manifests. A malicious or accidental manifest change can redirect delivery or expose private media even without compromising storage itself.

Protect unreleased assets through access controls, watermarking where appropriate, and carefully scoped partner delivery. A content hash verifies bytes but does not establish that the person submitting them had authority to publish.

Abuse and resilience

Apply rate limits and admission controls to expensive endpoints. Use layered DDoS protection and isolate abusive traffic without making a single global challenge service a critical dependency for all playback. Preserve accessibility and recovery paths for legitimate users incorrectly flagged by automated systems.

Validation gate

Threat-model stolen upload URLs, compromised encoder workers, leaked stream keys, malicious subtitles, account recovery abuse, signing-key rotation, and unauthorized support actions. Run independent security review and red-team exercises before production; passing local correctness tests is not a security certification.

Back to contents

Infrastructure, reliability, and operating design

CHAPTER 63

Capacity planning and cost models

Use explicit units and scenario assumptions instead of borrowing headline scale numbers.

Scope

All workloads and costs in this chapter are illustrative planning scenarios. They are not YouTube traffic, infrastructure counts, supplier prices, or operating expenses. Public upload and view statistics use different definitions and should not be combined casually to infer a hidden workload.

A worked ingest scenario

Assume 100,000 uploaded videos per day, averaging six minutes at 12 Mbps source bitrate. Source ingress is approximately 100,000 * 360 * 12 / 8 = 54,000,000 MB, or 54 TB per day using decimal units. That is about 5 Gbps average ingress before peaks and overhead. A four-times peak assumption implies 20 Gbps before protocol and resilience margin.

The platform receives 600,000 source minutes per day. If the aggregate encoding work averages eight compute-minutes per source minute across all selected outputs, that is 4.8 million compute-minutes daily. At 60% effective utilization, approximately 5,556 continuously available reference compute slots are needed. The "slot" must be calibrated by real benchmarks; it is not automatically one CPU core.

A worked delivery scenario

Assume one million concurrent viewers at an average delivered rate of 3 Mbps. Media egress is 3 Tbps. If sustained for an hour, that is about 1.35 PB of decimal data before overhead. A small bitrate change therefore has large network consequences, while cache placement changes where that traffic travels rather than eliminating the viewer's last-mile bytes.

With four-second video segments, those viewers generate roughly 250,000 video-segment requests per second, plus audio, manifests, retries, and other traffic. Lower-latency segmentation can multiply request load without changing average media bitrate.

Storage growth

If retained derivatives add 1.5 times source size and sources are retained, logical media growth is 135 TB per day in this scenario. Physical capacity then depends on replication or coding, old releases, failed attempts, metadata, and retention. Do not multiply by a vague "three replicas" when the chosen system uses a different redundancy policy.

Cost equation

Estimate compute, storage, network delivery, inter-region transfer, cache hardware or CDN fees, observability, support, moderation, rights operations, and partner costs separately. Use current supplier quotes when making financial commitments. This book provides formulas, not invented per-unit prices.

Sensitivity and headroom

Vary average duration, codec mix, derivative count, concurrency, bitrate, cache hit rate, and utilization. Reserve headroom for a failure domain loss and a popularity spike occurring together. The synthetic charts show how these assumptions change capacity; they are planning tools rather than measured production curves.

Back to contents

Infrastructure, reliability, and operating design

CHAPTER 64

Team ownership and the operating company

A video platform is an engineering and operations organization, not just a deployed codebase.

Proposed ownership map

Create clear owners for creator ingest, media processing, playback clients, delivery, discovery, community, rights and safety, monetization, data/ML, platform reliability, and security. Early teams may combine several domains, but each production invariant still needs one accountable owner.

Interfaces between teams

The media team guarantees validated immutable releases. The publication team guarantees atomic selection and versioning. The policy team guarantees decision semantics and freshness. The delivery team guarantees bounded serving behavior for authorized objects. The client team measures actual playback outcomes. These contracts prevent incidents from becoming arguments about whose dashboard is green.

Maintain service catalogs with owners, dependencies, SLOs, runbooks, data classifications, and escalation paths. A service without an on-call owner or rollback procedure is not ready to become a critical dependency.

Human operations

Creator support, copyright review, safety escalation, advertiser operations, and financial reconciliation are part of the system. Give them purpose-built tools, audit trails, and queue visibility. Manual database edits are not a scalable operations strategy.

Design review capacity alongside automated detection. A model that sends every uncertain case to humans can overwhelm the queue. Measure arrival rate, handling time, backlog age, and appeal outcomes. Use staffing and tooling to maintain a humane, reliable process rather than optimizing only cases closed per hour.

Partner ecosystem

A new company needs content and music rights expertise, payment and advertising partners, device testing, accessibility review, legal counsel, and security assessment. Building technology does not grant distribution rights or regulatory compliance. Contracts determine important engineering requirements such as retention, reporting, entitlements, and takedown response.

Build versus buy

Initially buy commodity storage, CDN delivery, identity foundations, payment processing, and perhaps transcoding. Own the differentiated creator workflow, catalog, publication semantics, discovery experience, and measurement definitions. Replace suppliers only when economics, control, or reliability justify the operational burden.

Incident culture

Run blameless technical reviews that still assign concrete corrective ownership. Record contributing conditions, missed signals, decision timing, and why safeguards failed. Track completion of fixes and repeat drills. A postmortem that ends with "be more careful" has not changed the system.

Launch gate

Before expanding a market or product, verify rights and policy readiness, support language coverage, payment and reporting capability, device compatibility, abuse controls, and recovery drills. Engineering readiness and company readiness must advance together.

Implementation roadmap and worked incidents

CHAPTER 65

Build the company in evidence-driven stages

Sequence the risks so the first launch teaches you what to build next.

Stage 1: a coherent vertical slice

Build account and channel ownership, resumable upload, quarantined source storage, one compatible encoding path, a validated release, controlled publication, basic playback, and deletion. Use a transactional database, managed object storage, a durable queue, and a commercial CDN. Keep a small service count and strong module boundaries.

The acceptance test is not "a video played once." It is a video that uploads through disconnects, survives a worker crash, publishes once after a lost response, plays on the supported devices, and becomes unavailable according to the documented withdrawal bound. Instrument the whole journey before adding sophisticated discovery.

Stage 2: creators and operational trust

Add Studio workflows, captions, multiple representations, basic search, subscriptions, comments, moderation queues, rights evidence, and creator support. Establish audit trails and a real incident process. Introduce public integration APIs only with quotas, idempotency, deprecation policy, and abuse controls.

At this stage, a simple relevance model and managed infrastructure are usually more valuable than custom hardware or a global database. Measure where users fail and where costs accumulate. Do not split the catalog into many services merely to imitate a large company's historical architecture.

Stage 3: scale and monetization

Add stronger recommendation models, richer analytics, advertising or subscriptions, creator allocation, and financial reconciliation. Build consent-aware feature pipelines and metric definitions. Separate provisional reporting from finalized obligations. Add cells or shards only after load and organizational ownership justify them.

Monetization should not precede auditable measurement. Paying creators from an approximate public counter creates a financial correctness problem that becomes harder to repair as the business grows.

Stage 4: live and advanced products

Introduce live streaming with rehearsed source redundancy, epoch fencing, DVR policy, chat backpressure, and event operations. Add regional recovery with explicit authority transfer. Expand localization, shopping, music, television, or games as separate product programs with their own rights and support requirements.

Stage 5: infrastructure differentiation

Consider proprietary cache placement, advanced learned eviction, specialized encoding hardware, or a large internal data platform only when measured economics and scale justify ownership. Build a business case including engineering, maintenance, supply chain, operations, and exit strategy, not just benchmark efficiency.

Decision gates

Each stage needs a correctness gate, a user-experience gate, an operational gate, and a commercial/legal gate. Progress is based on evidence: successful recovery drills, observed tail latency, reconciled financial periods, supported devices, and manageable review backlogs. A feature checklist without those gates is not a production roadmap.

Back to contents

Implementation roadmap and worked incidents

CHAPTER 66

Worked journey: upload, publish, watch, and withdraw

Trace one video through uncertain acknowledgments and changing authority.

Scenario

A creator uploads a twelve-minute tutorial, publishes it after processing, corrects its captions, and later makes it private. The network drops responses at two inconvenient points. All identifiers and times below are illustrative.

09:00 - interrupted upload

The server acknowledges chunks through byte offset 67,108,864. The next chunk reaches durable storage and its receipt commits, but the response is lost. The client queries the upload session rather than guessing. The server reports the next expected offset. The client resumes from that point, and final length and digest validation seal asset-A.

The upload operation now says SEALED; the video is still a draft. No search index or player should infer publication from the existence of the source object.

09:02 - processing and a stale worker

Workflow W1 creates a baseline encode, audio, thumbnails, and captions. One high-quality encode attempt stalls. A replacement receives generation 8. When the old generation 7 worker later finishes, its output can be retained temporarily but cannot become the selected result. The release validator assembles release-R1 from approved objects.

09:06 - publication response lost

The creator submits publication key publish-42 with expected video revision 3 and release R1. The transaction commits revision 4, its audit record, and an outbox event. The response disappears. Retrying the same key and payload returns revision 4. Fanout and search consumers may see duplicate events, but their stable event identity prevents duplicate feed entries.

09:07 - first playback

A viewer sees a search result, but the playback service independently checks current availability. It issues a short-lived grant for R1 and a compatible track set. Media comes from an edge cache. The recommendation service can fail without stopping this already selected playback.

09:10 - caption correction

The creator corrects a caption track. A new validated release R2 references the unchanged video objects and the corrected caption object. New sessions select R2. Existing R1 sessions remain coherent; the system does not mutate caption bytes behind the old URL. If the correction were safety-critical, policy could require those sessions to refresh sooner.

09:12 - private transition

The creator changes visibility to private. The authoritative policy version advances, new public grants are denied, and derived surfaces receive removal events. Existing grants retain only their documented bounded authority; deny propagation may shorten that window. Already delivered bytes cannot be recalled.

What to verify

The final state has one sealed source, explainable releases, one publication effect for the retried command, current private authority, and no stale worker or replay capable of republishing the video. Search freshness, cache purging, and access revocation are measured separately rather than reported as one ambiguous "delete complete" flag.

Back to contents

Implementation roadmap and worked incidents

CHAPTER 67

Worked incident: live failover after an uncertain commit

Preserve one public timeline while two regions disagree about what happened.

Scenario

A live broadcast uses primary publisher P in region A and a backup source in region B. The current publication epoch is 17. P submits video segment sequence 8,401, then loses connectivity before receiving the commit response. The media objects already exist in durable storage.

Establish facts before retrying

The operator sees a timeout, not proof of failure. The authority service is queried for (broadcast, 17, video, 8401). If the selection exists, its digest is authoritative. If it does not, an authorized publisher may retry under the defined epoch. A new sequence number must not be invented merely to escape uncertainty.

The player manifest advances only from committed selections. Some viewers may temporarily remain one segment behind, but they should not receive two different objects under the same immutable segment identity.

Transfer authority

Region A remains partitioned, so the coordinator promotes a new publisher with epoch 18 using the chosen consistent authority mechanism. The commit service rejects any later write carrying epoch 17. This is essential because P may resume and still believe it owns the stream.

The backup source is not assumed to be byte-identical. The new publisher verifies its presentation timeline, codec initialization, audio alignment, and a safe random-access boundary. It records a discontinuity where needed and publishes the new epoch's manifest version.

Control the viewer experience

Players refresh manifests and follow the explicit timeline transition. Some may need extra buffer or a decoder reset. Measure recovery duration, live latency, stalls, and error cohorts. Do not hide a discontinuity by reusing old timestamps; that can create a more severe playback failure.

Chat remains on its own log and reconnect protocol. Paid interactions retain their financial identities even if fanout is delayed. A media failover does not authorize duplicate charges or duplicate creator allocation.

Protect the archive

The final recording follows committed segment selections from epochs 17 and 18. Unselected candidate objects are not automatically appended. The archive builder validates continuity and produces a new on-demand release with explicit gaps or edits where necessary.

Recovery of region A

Before region A rejoins, it learns the current epoch and discards its obsolete write authority. Its local pending jobs reconcile against committed selections. It may contribute read capacity or new work only after state and configuration checks pass.

Incident review

Determine why the acknowledgment became uncertain, whether failover waited too long or acted too early, whether the backup was truly independent, and whether cache and player behavior matched the rehearsal. The key correctness result is one selected timeline with bounded interruption, not a claim that redundancy made the event failure-free.

Back to contents

Implementation roadmap and worked incidents

CHAPTER 68

Runbooks and the production-readiness gate

Every architecture claim should have a test, an owner, and an action when it fails.

Upload and processing incident

When upload completion stalls, distinguish ingress loss, missing receipts, verification failure, and queue delay. Preserve sealed assets; do not ask creators to re-upload until the service has checked durable state. For processing backlog, inspect work-seconds, oldest age, resource class, and deterministic failures. Pause optional re-encodes before starving baseline readiness.

Playback incident

Start from user impact: failed starts, stalls, codec errors, or one network cohort. Compare authorization, manifest, cache, transport, and decoder signals. Roll back a bad recipe or steering change with a known-good release. Do not disable permission checks as a general availability fix.

Rights or privacy incident

Commit current deny state first, stop issuing affected grants, verify propagation, and remove derived discovery entries. Track the actual residual-authority bound and previously delivered-data limitation. Preserve narrowly scoped evidence under restricted access. Do not claim completion from a cache purge alone.

Live incident

Establish ingest health, selected segment progress, current epoch, and viewer playback. Transfer authority only through the defined fencing mechanism. Use a tested backup and explicit timeline discontinuity. Reduce nonessential interaction load before sacrificing the media path. Keep communication accurate about observed impact and unresolved uncertainty.

Financial incident

Freeze affected finalization or payout batches without losing immutable input evidence. Reconcile event IDs, allocation versions, journal postings, and partner references. Never repair a discrepancy by directly editing historical totals until they "look right." Use reviewed correcting entries and explain creator-facing changes.

Readiness evidence

A production launch requires protocol and device compatibility, upload and publication fault tests, verified revocation bounds, live failover rehearsals where applicable, data restoration, financial reconciliation, privacy deletion tests, security review, and operational staffing. Each item has a named owner and an artifact that demonstrates the result.

The companion's local tests are educational evidence for selected transaction and algorithm properties. They do not establish distributed consensus, global durability, real-device performance, legal compliance, licensed content protection, or security certification. Those need implementation-specific review and independent testing.

Final design principle

Keep observations, proposals, commitments, permissions, bytes, and financial outcomes distinct. Connect them with explicit identities, versions, and evidence. This allows the platform to improve quality, personalize discovery, and scale delivery without losing the ability to explain what happened when a request, model, network, or human process fails.

Implementation appendices

APPENDIX A

Logical data model and transaction boundaries

Forty-eight logical entities; a smaller executable schema demonstrates selected invariants.

Scope and conventions

This is a proposed model, not YouTube's physical schema. Logical entities can share tables initially and split later when access patterns justify it. Every mutable authoritative row has an expected version; every asynchronous artifact records its input and recipe versions. Identifiers are opaque and scoped where needed. Time intervals specify inclusivity and units.

Entity Principal key Authority and invariant
Account account_id Personal identity; not interchangeable with a channel.
Channel channel_id Creator-facing ownership and publication boundary.
ChannelMembership channel_id, actor_id Role, scope, validity, and relation version.
CapabilityDecision subject, context, version Region, audience, surface, and feature eligibility.
Video video_id Stable work identity and current metadata version.
VideoMetadataRevision video_id, revision Immutable record of title, description, and settings.
UploadSession upload_id Owner, total length, durable offset, expiry, state.
ChunkReceipt upload_id, offset One accepted length and digest for a byte range.
SourceAsset asset_id Sealed source length, checksum, and provenance.
ProbeResult asset_id, probe_version Track/timeline description and validation result.
MediaWorkflow workflow_id Source, recipe set, logical operation, and status.
Job job_id Dependencies, selected result, deadline, generation.
JobAttempt job_id, generation Fenced execution and attempt-specific outputs.
MediaObject object_digest Immutable bytes, length, storage and integrity metadata.
Representation representation_id Codec, dimensions, timeline, and object references.
AudioTrack audio_track_id Language, provenance, consent, timing, and review state.
CaptionTrack caption_track_id Text/timing revision and source timeline.
MediaRelease release_id Validated coherent collection of immutable assets.
ReleaseObject release_id, object_id Reference graph used by validation and collection.
Publication video_id, publication_revision Selected release, visibility, and causal policy bound.
PolicyDecision resource, policy_version Scope, reason, evidence, effective time, and deny state.
PlaybackSession session_id Selected release and client capability context.
PlaybackGrant grant_id Bounded permission, audience, tracks, and expiry.
OfflinePackage package_id Device/account scope and refresh/expiry conditions.
ProgressState account_id, video_id Intent generation, sequence, and resume position.
HistoryConsent account_id, generation Collection permission and deletion watermark.
SubscriptionRelation viewer_id, channel_id Current relation and notification preference version.
FeedEntry recipient, publication_event Derived, deduplicated discovery entry.
NotificationAttempt event_id, destination Delivery state independent of feed existence.
Comment comment_id Body revision, parent, moderation and deletion state.
Reaction actor, object, kind Idempotent current user reaction.
Playlist playlist_id Visibility, owner, and ordered-list revision.
PlaylistItem playlist_id, item_id Stable occurrence identity and sequence position.
Broadcast broadcast_id Lifecycle, schedule, and current publication epoch.
IngestSession ingest_id Source generation, credentials, and health.
SegmentSelection broadcast, epoch, track, sequence One immutable selected digest.
ChatMessage chat_id, message_id Ordered content plus moderation tombstones.
RightsReference reference_id Partner asset, ownership assertion, and territory.
RightsMatch match_id Detector evidence and matched intervals, not legal proof.
RightsCase case_id Claims, evidence, actors, deadlines, and decisions.
AdOpportunity opportunity_id Permitted context and deduplicated request identity.
AdDecision decision_id Creative, campaign, eligibility, and pricing version.
QualifiedEvent event_id, definition_version Validated measurement with explicit semantics.
RevenueAllocation period, creator, rule_version Reproducible allocation and adjustment lineage.
Journal journal_id Immutable balanced postings in a named currency.
PayoutInstruction instruction_id Partner reference and uncertain/confirmed outcome.
OutboxEvent event_id Atomic bridge from authoritative mutation to events.
ConsumerReceipt consumer, event_id Deduplication tied to a projection's transaction.

Example SQL constraints

The following excerpts illustrate constraints. They omit production indexes, migration management, partitioning, encryption, and many fields. The companion schema.sql contains the executable SQLite teaching schema, not this entire logical model.

CREATE TABLE chunk_receipt (
  upload_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  byte_offset BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (byte_offset >= 0),
  byte_length BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (byte_length > 0),
  sha256 TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (upload_id, byte_offset)
);

CREATE TABLE segment_selection (
  broadcast_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  publication_epoch BIGINT NOT NULL,
  track_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  sequence_no BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (sequence_no >= 0),
  object_digest TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (broadcast_id, publication_epoch, track_id, sequence_no)
);

CREATE TABLE consumer_receipt (
  consumer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  event_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  payload_digest TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (consumer_name, event_id)
);

A uniqueness constraint prevents two selected rows for one key, but does not alone prevent a stale writer from creating a new sequence. The commit transaction must also check the current broadcast epoch. A foreign key can ensure a release exists, but does not prove it passed media validation; the publication transaction must check that state and its version.

Index design

Use (channel_id, published_at, video_id) for creator listings; (video_id, revision) for metadata history; (state, next_attempt_at) for runnable jobs; (aggregate_id, version) for ordered event reconciliation; and (creator_id, period, status) for financial statements. Avoid low-selectivity indexes that amplify writes without serving a measured query.

Large media never belongs in ordinary metadata rows. The teaching model stores tiny chunk bytes in SQLite solely to make rollback and integrity tests self-contained. Production chunks should be durable objects with receipts that refer to them. That introduces an object-store/database boundary requiring reconciliation, as described in Chapter 9.

Transaction ownership

Publication pointer, idempotency response, audit, and outbox belong together. Consumer receipt and projection effect belong together. Journal header and postings belong together. Expensive encoding, third-party notifications, and bank settlement do not fit inside those transactions. Model them as durable work with explicit external identities and recovery.

Implementation appendices

APPENDIX B

Proposed API contracts and integration rules

These endpoints belong to the reference platform, not to YouTube's public or private API.

Endpoint Contract Important failure behavior
POST /v1/channels/{c}/uploads Create scoped upload session with declared size. Idempotency key; quota and capability check.
PUT /v1/uploads/{u}/chunks Submit offset, length, digest, and bytes. Exact retry accepted; gap or conflicting bytes rejected.
GET /v1/uploads/{u} Return durable offset and state. Must remain available under upload throttling.
POST /v1/uploads/{u}:seal Verify and seal immutable source. Incomplete or mismatched digest cannot seal.
POST /v1/videos Create draft bound to channel and source. Does not imply processing or publication.
PATCH /v1/videos/{v} Apply metadata under expected revision. Stale revision returns conflict.
POST /v1/videos/{v}/workflows Start processing with immutable recipe set. Returns operation; duplicate command returns same work.
GET /v1/operations/{o} Read logical job progress and result. Attempt retries do not change operation identity.
POST /v1/videos/{v}:publish Select validated release and visibility. Atomic state, response, audit, and outbox.
POST /v1/videos/{v}:withdraw Advance deny/visibility generation. Return propagation status separately from commit.
POST /v1/playback-sessions Evaluate current policy and capabilities. Bounded grant; no arbitrary object path input.
PUT /v1/progress/{v} Write generation, sequence, and position. Old generation/sequence cannot overwrite new intent.
POST /v1/broadcasts Create scheduled live control resource. Ingest connection alone does not make it live.
POST /v1/broadcasts/{b}:transition Versioned testing/live/complete command. Invalid lifecycle transition rejected.
POST /v1/rights-cases/{r}:respond Add authorized evidence or decision. Case version and deadline generation enforced.
GET /v1/creator-reports Authorized dimensions and metrics. Definition version, freshness, and provisional flag.

Publication example

POST /v1/videos/vid_42:publish
Authorization: Bearer <scoped-credential>
Idempotency-Key: pub_2026_09_27_01
If-Match: "video-version-12"
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "release_id": "rel_8",
  "visibility": "PUBLIC",
  "schedule_generation": 3
}

{
  "video_id": "vid_42",
  "publication_revision": 13,
  "release_id": "rel_8",
  "operation_id": "op_pub_51",
  "discovery_propagation": "PENDING"
}

The response says the authoritative publication committed. It does not promise every search index or subscriber device has observed it. A retry with the same key returns this historical result, even if a later command has since withdrawn the video; returning the old result must not reapply the old publication. Clients needing current state should read the resource.

Error envelope

{
  "error": {
    "code": "VERSION_CONFLICT",
    "message": "The video changed after this draft was loaded.",
    "retryable": false,
    "request_id": "req_8",
    "current_revision": 14
  }
}

Do not reveal current_revision or resource existence to unauthorized callers. A retryable error includes a bounded retry-after hint when useful. A validation error should identify actionable fields without exposing private infrastructure details.

Pagination and streaming

Use opaque cursors tied to sort order and filter context. Changing filters invalidates the cursor. For live chat, reconnect with a continuation token and deduplicate by message ID; an expired cursor should produce an explicit resynchronization path. Public YouTube integrations should use the documented streamList behavior rather than assuming this reference API exists. [22]

Security and compatibility

Require HTTPS, scoped credentials, audience validation, and object-level authorization on every request. Check role and channel scope again for mutations. Version schemas and semantics; document deprecation periods and supported client behavior. Test quota exhaustion, partial batch outcomes, lost responses, and old clients as first-class API cases.

Implementation appendices

APPENDIX C

Eight critical algorithms

Language-neutral pseudocode makes the commit points and failure assumptions visible.

C1. Accept an upload chunk

validate nonnegative offset, positive length, declared digest
lookup session in caller's channel scope
reject expired or aborted session
if receipt exists at offset:
    require identical length and digest
    return durable next offset
require OPEN and offset == durable next offset
require offset + length <= declared total
write immutable staged chunk; verify length and digest
transaction:
    lock session; recheck state, expiry, and offset
    insert unique chunk receipt
    advance durable next offset
commit, then acknowledge

The staged object write is outside the metadata transaction. A crash can leave an orphan object, which reconciliation may reuse or collect. It must not leave an acknowledged offset without a durable verified object. Production implementations must specify the storage durability acknowledgment they rely on.

C2. Publish a media release

authorize actor for channel and publish action
canonical_hash = hash(meaningful command fields)
transaction:
    look up scoped idempotency key
    if present: require same hash; return recorded result
    lock video; require expected metadata version
    require current schedule generation and allowed policy state
    require selected release belongs to video and is VALIDATED
    update publication pointer and increment revision
    append audit and outbox event
    store idempotency result
commit, then return

Check authorization before returning sensitive stored responses. An idempotent retry retrieves the prior command's outcome, not the current resource state. It must never rerun a publication after a later withdrawal.

C3. Create a bounded playback grant

read video and selected release at a coherent version
obtain authorization at required causal consistency bound
require current deny freshness within configured maximum
check audience, territory, entitlement, and device compatibility
select allowed tracks and release
create signed grant with resource, audience, policy version, expiry
record minimal session evidence
return manifest description and delivery endpoints

If current deny freshness cannot be established, do not issue new unrestricted authority. A signed token is only as trustworthy as the state used to mint it. Edge checks and refresh policies determine the residual revocation bound.

C4. Select a live segment

write candidate object under immutable digest; verify durability
transaction:
    read current publication epoch for broadcast
    require caller epoch == current epoch
    key = (broadcast, epoch, track, sequence)
    if selection exists:
        require identical digest; return existing selection
    validate timeline and codec prerequisites
    insert unique selection
    append manifest-update outbox event
commit, then acknowledge

A timed-out old publisher may still run, so epoch checks occur at commit. A failover can require a new timeline discontinuity. The model does not infer that two redundant encoder outputs are byte-identical.

C5. Apply progress without losing a rewind

require position >= 0 and sequence >= 0
transaction:
    load progress for account and video
    require command generation == current intent generation
    if sequence <= stored sequence: ignore as stale/duplicate
    write position and sequence, even when position decreases
commit

A new device or explicit reset obtains a server-controlled generation according to the product's conflict policy. Client wall time alone is not a reliable total order. History deletion advances a suppression generation so old buffered updates cannot resurrect it.

C6. Apply a projection event once

transaction:
    if (consumer, event_id) receipt exists:
        require same payload digest; return duplicate
    check aggregate version and deletion generation
    insert receipt
    apply deterministic projection effect
    update durable consumer progress where compatible
commit

This gives one local transactional effect, not universal exactly-once delivery. External notifications or partner APIs require their own idempotency and outcome records. A broker acknowledgment does not prove those effects occurred.

C7. Allocate a finite revenue pool

freeze eligible inputs, period, territory, currency, and rule version
compute eligible weights using defined qualified measures
if total weight == 0: follow explicit unallocated-pool policy
calculate exact rational allocation for each eligible creator
round down to currency minor units
distribute remaining units by deterministic remainder ordering
require sum(allocations) == distributable pool
post uniquely identified balanced journals

This is a generic finite-pool algorithm, not the complete Shorts commercial formula. Licensing, eligibility, taxes, contracts, and holds determine the actual distributable base. Re-running the same immutable input set must not create another payable.

C8. Make a conservative ABR choice

observe recent completed transfers and buffer level
estimate conservative useful throughput
enumerate device-compatible representations
for each candidate:
    predict next-segment download time including overhead
    estimate stall risk and quality benefit
reject candidates outside buffer/latency/data constraints
choose highest acceptable utility with switching hysteresis
on uncertainty: prefer a compatible lower-cost representation
request media; update observations after completion

This is not a production optimizer. Real implementations need variable segment sizes, transport behavior, decoder limits, abandonment, live-edge control, and user preferences. The synthetic lab makes only the buffer arithmetic and feedback intuition executable.
